source: Liu et al. (2025 update) GLoRE: reasoning models on logical-reading benchmarks
finding: Reasoning models now far exceed the old GPT-4 numbers on AR-LSAT, ReClor and LogiQA 2.0. AR-LSAT, once the hardest item set, is at or above the human ceiling for two models.
numbers: Table 2, accuracy %. AR-LSAT: GPT-4 73.12, o1-mini 79.23, DeepSeek-R1 90.01, QwQ-32B 92.35 (human avg 56, ceiling 91). ReClor dev (500): GPT-4 87.20, o1-mini 80.57, R1 77.88, QwQ 93.76. LogiQA 2.0 en: GPT-4 72.25, o1-mini 69.35, R1 76.22, QwQ 85.70 (human 86, ceiling 95).
quote: QwQ-32B attains the highest average accuracy (78.95%)
limits: GLoRE's GPT-4 AR-LSAT of 73.12 conflicts with 33-43 in Liu 2023 and Logic-LM (different prompt and set; 230 items). One run per model, no error bars. Baselines are prompt-dependent.
agent_relevance: AR-LSAT and ReClor are close to saturated for reasoning models, so a scaffold gain on them is hard to see. Use post-cutoff items and LogiEval-Hard.

source: Liu et al. GLoRE: LogiQA22 (2022 exam items) versus LogiQA 2.0
finding: On the newer LogiQA22 set (1,354 items from 2022 exams, outside the original dataset) older models drop; reasoning models hold up better. The drop hints at memory or distribution shift.
numbers: GPT-4 58.49 on LogiQA22 vs 72.25 on LogiQA 2.0 (-13.8). DeepSeek-R1 71.63 vs 76.22. QwQ-32B 86.30 vs 85.70. o1-mini 59.84 vs 69.35. Human avg 83, ceiling 99 on LogiQA22.
quote: GPT-4's accuracy drops significantly on LogiQA22
limits: The drop could be contamination, a harder item mix, or distribution shift. No contamination test was run. One run per model.
agent_relevance: LogiQA22 is a usable post-cutoff probe for older models but is itself dated 2022; frontier 2025-26 models may have seen it.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Evaluating the Logical Reasoning Abilities of Large Reasoning Models (LogiEval)
finding: LogiEval has 6,235 items from LSAT, GMAT, civil-service and other exams. Seven reasoning models cluster at 78.7-81.4% overall. They beat humans on 4-choice argument analysis and fail on 5-option items.
numbers: Total accuracy 78.74% to 81.41% (DeepSeek-R1 best, 81.41%). 4-choice argument analysis: humans 85.2%, models 81.20-89.90% (o4-mini 89.90). 5-option items: Grok3-Think 51.86%, o4-mini 54.85%, DeepSeek-R1 73.38%. Essential-part items: all 95%+ vs human 92.3%.
limits: Models: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Grok3, o4-mini, Qwen3-235B, QwQ-32B. Human numbers are historical passing rates, not same-sitting data. One run per item.
agent_relevance: Format effects (4 vs 5 options) are large, so an S0 gate must fix option count and shuffle options.

source: Liu et al. (2025) LogiEval-Hard subset
finding: Items that a small model (Qwen3-30B-A3B) fails three times also defeat large models. This gives a hard, unsaturated subset.
numbers: LogiEval-Hard = 1,617 items; average model accuracy 37.97%, below 40% for all models. 18.3% of all items were missed by every model; errors concentrate in abductive reasoning (32% of the hard subset) and situational judgement (27%).
limits: Selected by adversarial filtering against a small model, so selection bias and some label errors inflate apparent difficulty (annotators checked a sample only).
agent_relevance: Best candidate S0 gate set for a 2026 agent: unsaturated, mixed reasoning types, 1,617 items allow a powered test.

source: Liu et al. (2025) LogiEval: human difficulty versus model accuracy
finding: Human difficulty does not predict model difficulty. Models solved items humans mostly fail and missed items humans mostly pass.
numbers: Table 4, n=7 items per band: human 18% -> model 85.71% (p=0.0032); human 31% -> 0.00%; human 41% -> 100%; human 46% -> 28.57%; human 85% -> 100%.
limits: Only 7 items per band: very low power; illustrative, not a test.
agent_relevance: Do not use human norms as a difficulty scale for our agent's gate; calibrate on model pass rates.

source: Miller (2024) Adding Error Bars to Evals
finding: Gives a sample-size formula for detecting a gain between two models on the same eval. A 3-point gain needs about 970 independent items under stated assumptions.
numbers: Paired design, deterministic answers, paired-difference variance 1/9, alpha 0.05, power 80%, delta 0.03: n = (z0.025+z0.20)^2 (1/9)/0.03^2 = about 969. Authors suggest new evals hold at least 1,000 questions.
quote: new evals should contain at least 1,000 questions in order to have good signaling ability
limits: Parameters are described as fictional but reasonable. Real variance depends on the score correlation between arms; higher correlation lowers n.
agent_relevance: Answers the N question: for a 3-point scaffold gain plan roughly 1,000 paired items, not 100-200.

source: Miller (2024) Adding Error Bars to Evals: resampling and minimum detectable effect
finding: Resampling each question K times cuts sampling noise but not the noise from which questions were chosen. Paired comparison is a free variance reduction.
numbers: Variance factor (1+2/K)/3 in the worked example: K=2 cuts total variance by 1/3, K=4 by 1/2, K=6 by 5/9, limit 2/3. With n=198, alpha .05, power 80%, corr .5, going from K=1 to K=10 reduces minimum detectable effect from 13.2% to 7.5%.
limits: Worked example assumes a simple score model. Real evals differ.
agent_relevance: With a 198-item set even 10 repeats cannot resolve below 7.5 points; plan item count, not repeats.

source: Miller (2024) Adding Error Bars to Evals: clustered items
finding: When items come in groups (several questions per passage, as in LSAT reading comprehension and logic games), naive standard errors are too small.
numbers: Clustered standard errors can be up to 3x the naive ones on real evals (Table 4, DROP and another eval, Anthropic models).
limits: Shown on reading-comprehension evals, not on LSAT directly.
agent_relevance: LSAT RC and AR-LSAT have several questions per passage or game: cluster by passage when computing error bars.

source: Atil et al. (2025) Non-Determinism of 'Deterministic' LLM Settings
finding: At temperature 0, top-p 1, fixed seed, identical inputs still give different outputs. Accuracy varies across runs for five LLMs on eight tasks.
numbers: 10 runs per condition: accuracy variation up to 15% across runs; best-possible minus worst-possible accuracy up to 70%. Parsed answers far more stable than raw strings (TARa@10 vs TARr@10). No model repeated accuracy across all tasks. No chain-of-thought used.
quote: accuracy variations up to 15% across naturally occurring runs
limits: Tasks were BBH and MMLU subsets, not CT tests. Answer extraction partly hard-coded. The 70% best-worst gap is an upper extreme.
agent_relevance: Temperature 0 is not a noise-free baseline. Run the plain arm several times and report the spread before claiming a scaffold gain.

source: Pezeshkpour and Hruschka (2024) LLMs sensitivity to the order of options in multiple-choice questions
finding: Shuffling answer options changes accuracy a lot. The sensitivity gap (best vs worst oracle order) is large for GPT-4 and InstructGPT, and few-shot demos do not remove it.
numbers: Table 1 (zero-shot, GPT-4 columns): Professional Law 57.0 with -30.0 / +23.0 under worst / best ordering. Positional calibration gave up to 8 points improvement.
limits: Gap measured with oracle ordering (knows the truth), so it is an upper bound on practical swing. Pre-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Fix and shuffle option order across repeated runs; report accuracy averaged over permutations.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically
finding: Instruction in critical thinking raises standardised CT test scores by a modest, heterogeneous amount. Dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring help.
numbers: 341 effect sizes from quasi- or true-experimental studies; weighted random-effects mean g+ = 0.30 (p < .001), heterogeneous (p < .001).
quote: The weighted random effects mean effect size (g+) was 0.30
limits: Only the abstract was opened (full text paywalled). Design quality varies.
agent_relevance: Human reference scale: 0.30 SD is a typical instruction effect.

source: Huber and Kuncel (2016) Does College Teach Critical Thinking? A Meta-Analysis
finding: CT skills and dispositions improve substantially over a normal college experience. Curriculum-wide efforts do not yield larger long-term gains.
numbers: 71 research reports over 48 years; four-year gain equals moving from the 50th to the 72nd percentile (about 0.58 SD by normal conversion). Gains have fallen over time. Nursing programs that stress CT showed no extra gain.
limits: Read via the AERA summary and the journal abstract; the full effect-size table (per-year d, skills vs dispositions) was not opened. Gain is not causal to instruction (maturation, selection).
agent_relevance: Supports the earlier recalled ~0.5 SD; four years of college is about 0.5-0.6 SD, a scale for what counts as large.

source: Arum and Roksa (2011) Academically Adrift (CLA longitudinal)
finding: Across the first two years, many students show no measured gain on the Collegiate Learning Assessment.
numbers: More than 2,300 undergraduates at 24 institutions; 45% showed no significant improvement in critical thinking, complex reasoning and writing over the first two years (publisher abstract).
limits: Abstract only. The 45% depends on the individual-level reliability of CLA change scores, which is limited; the 2016 meta-analysis found larger average gains.
agent_relevance: Individual change scores on CT tests are noisy; judge a scaffold effect at group level.

source: Peczuh et al. (2025) Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
finding: LLM scoring of CT subskills in student essays reaches only moderate agreement with humans. Fine-tuned Llama 8B beat GPT-5 prompting.
numbers: 500 human-coded essays (of 4,115), subskill rubrics with 5 levels. Accuracy: Llama-8B fine-tuned .604, ModernBERT .563, GPT-5 zero-shot .543, GPT-5 few-shot .532; Krippendorff alpha .606 for Llama (only model above the .6 bar). Human coder group 2 weighted kappa means .69-.87 by subskill.
limits: Essays by grade 6-12 students; subtle or rare levels scored poorly (accuracy .39-.56 on unseen subskills). Single paper.
agent_relevance: Open-ended CT grading by an LLM judge is not yet at human-human reliability for fine levels; keep the S0 gate on closed-answer items.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: GPT-4 as judge agrees with human experts about as well as humans agree with each other, but has position and verbosity bias and weak math grading.
numbers: Agreement without ties: GPT-4 vs humans 85%, human vs human 81%. GPT-4 consistent under position swap in 65.0% of cases (default), 77.5% with few-shot. Humans judged GPT-4's disagreement reasonable in 75% of cases.
limits: Preference judgments on chat answers, not rubric scoring of CT essays. Old models.
agent_relevance: Use position swap and reference answers when an LLM grades the agent's critiques; do not trust one pass.

source: Castagna, Sassoon and Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought (CQoT)
finding: A pipeline asking Toulmin-style critical questions about the premises before answering gave about 5% higher judge scores than the baseline and plain CoT on MT-Bench reasoning and math.
numbers: Five LLMs (Llama 3.1-70B, Nemotron-51B, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Average gain vs baseline/CoT: +4.61% reasoning, +5.4% math. CQoT worse than CoT for Nemotron-51B on reasoning. Baselines often did better without CoT on MT-Bench reasoning.
limits: Not LSAT or ReClor. Judge was GPT-4o, scores 1-10, few questions; no significance tests; no equal-token control (CQoT uses several calls); MT-Bench may be contaminated. Authors suggest about 70B minimum.
agent_relevance: Weak support for critique-style prompting; the equal-token test on LSAT/ReClor-Hard with significance is still missing.

source: Self-Assessment Tests are Unreliable Measures of LLM Personality (BlackboxNLP 2024)
finding: Human self-report scales give unstable scores when given to LLMs: scores change with prompt wording and option order.
numbers: ChatGPT and three sizes of Llama2: three equivalent administrations gave large, mostly significant score differences; reordering answer options changed scores (ACL page summary; numbers not read).
limits: Only the ACL page summary was read, not the PDF. Personality, not CT dispositions.
agent_relevance: Disposition scales like CCTDI or Need for Cognition would likely be as unstable on LLMs; do not gate on them.

source: He and Liu (2025) Impact of LLM personality on cognitive bias manifestation
finding: Prompting LLMs with Big Five traits changes how strongly cognitive biases appear and how well debiasing prompts work. No Need for Cognition or CCTDI measure was used.
numbers: Eight biases, four LLMs: six prevalent biases; sunk cost and group attribution minimal. GPT-4 baseline bias 4.7%; Llama3-70B 91.23%. Conscientiousness and Agreeableness raised mitigation effect.
limits: Persona prompts, not a measured disposition. No correlation with accuracy on a skill test.
agent_relevance: No evidence that dispositional scores predict LLM task accuracy.

source: Absence search (second pass): Watson-Glaser, Cornell, CCTST, HCTA run on LLMs
finding: Two web searches and OpenAlex queries returned no study that gives a Watson-Glaser, Cornell or CCTST score for an LLM. Hits were about student use of ChatGPT and CT, or creativity tests (Torrance).
numbers: Zero direct hits across three query variants. Semantic Scholar and later OpenAlex calls were rate-limited.
limits: Absence of evidence: the instruments are commercial and copyrighted. Grey literature and SSRN were not searchable.
agent_relevance: Stay with open proxies (LSAT-family, LogiQA, ReClor, LogiEval, CRT).

source: Search (second pass) for 2025-26 frontier results on LogiQA, ReClor, AR-LSAT
finding: Reasoning-model numbers exist for early 2025 (GLoRE update, LogiEval) but no 2026 frontier numbers on AR-LSAT, LogiQA 2.0 or ReClor HARD were found; leaderboard aggregator pages are secondary and inconsistent.
numbers: Aggregator pages list GPT-4o LogiQA 56.3 and ReClor 72.4 with some obviously wrong entries. GLoRE gives R1 AR-LSAT 90.01. No plain-vs-scaffold comparison at equal tokens was found for these models.
limits: Search coverage limited by rate limits; ReClor HARD scores for reasoning models not found.
agent_relevance: The plain-vs-scaffold gap on current models is unmeasured; our own harness must measure it.
